title: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
summary: How to measure a retrieval system: test collections and pooling, precision and recall, average precision and MAP, MRR, graded nDCG, and the traps of judgment holes, query variance and tool defaults.
outcomes: Explain how a pooled test collection (topics, documents, qrels) is built and why unjudged documents bias scores
Compute precision, recall, P@k, R@k and F1 for a ranked list, and explain why accuracy fails for search
Compute average precision, MAP and MRR by hand and choose between them for a task
Compute DCG and nDCG with graded labels and explain why the ideal ranking comes from the qrels
Decide whether one system really beats another using per-query results and paired significance tests

lessons.title: Why you need a test collection before you can say better

blocks.md: You built a retrieval system on top of an inverted index with TF-IDF scoring. Now you change something: a new tokenizer, a different weighting, a reranker. You try five queries, three look better, two look worse. Is the change an improvement? Eyeballing a handful of queries cannot answer that, because results vary enormously from query to query and you remember the striking cases.

Search evaluation turns *is it better?* into a repeatable measurement. The standard recipe, called the **Cranfield paradigm** after the aerodynamics test collection built in the UK from the late 1950s, needs a **test collection** of three things:

1. A **document collection**.
2. A set of **information needs** (TREC calls them *topics*), each expressible as a query.
3. **Relevance judgments** (*qrels*): for each query and document pair, a human label, usually relevant or nonrelevant.

Relevance is judged against the **information need**, not the query words. A document that contains every query term can still be nonrelevant, and a document with none of them can be relevant. That is exactly why judgments must come from people and not from term matching.

Cranfield had 1398 abstracts and 225 queries, so every pair could be judged by hand. Modern collections have millions of documents, so judging every pair is impossible. TREC (run by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology since 1992) uses **pooling**: take the top-ranked documents from many different participating systems, merge them into a pool, and have assessors judge only the pool. Everything outside the pool is unjudged.

blocks.title: How a pooled test collection is built and used

nodes.label:
Pool: union of
each run's top docs

scenes.caption: Start with topics: written statements of an information need. Each one is turned into a query and sent to every participating system.
Each system returns a ranked list (a run). Only the top of each run goes into the pool, so the pool is far smaller than the collection.
Assessors judge only pooled documents against the full topic statement. Their labels become the qrels file.
Any run can now be scored automatically against the qrels, repeatably and cheaply. This reuse is the whole point of a test collection.
The catch: a new system D may retrieve documents no pooled system found. They are unjudged, and standard tools count them as nonrelevant, so D can be under-scored.

blocks.md: Human judges also disagree. Agreement is measured with Cohen's kappa (1 is perfect agreement, 0 is chance level), and TREC assessors typically land in the 0.67 to 0.8 range, only *fair* agreement. Experiments that swap one judge's labels for another's change absolute scores a lot but rarely change which system ranks above which. So test collections are trustworthy for **comparing systems**, much less for absolute numbers.

blocks.code:
# qrels file: query_id  iteration  doc_id  relevance
401 0 d14 1
401 0 d27 3
401 0 d9  2
401 0 d3  0

# run file: query_id  Q0  doc_id  rank  score  run_tag
401 Q0 d14 1 12.7 bm25
401 Q0 d3  2 11.9 bm25
401 Q0 d27 3 11.2 bm25
blocks.caption: The two plain-text formats trec_eval reads. Relevance 0 means judged nonrelevant; higher numbers are graded relevance.

blocks.md: trec_eval ignores the rank column of a run file. It sorts by the score column and breaks ties by document id, so a run whose scores disagree with its ranks gets evaluated in score order, not the order you intended.

One more rule from the start: if your system has knobs (like the weights or parameters of a ranking formula), tune them on a separate **development** set of queries and report results on the **test** set. Tuning on the test queries overstates performance, because the knobs fit those particular queries rather than queries in general.

blocks.question: System D is a new dense retriever evaluated on an old pooled collection. 30% of its top-10 documents were never judged. With default trec_eval settings, what happens to those documents?
options: They are skipped, and precision is computed only over judged documents
They are counted as nonrelevant, which can make D look worse than it is
They are counted as relevant, since the system found them
trec_eval refuses to score the run until they are judged
blocks.explain: trec_eval treats documents missing from the qrels like judged-nonrelevant ones. Skipping them is only done with the -J flag, which its own help text warns against using casually. If D finds relevant documents the pool missed, it gets no credit, so its score is biased downward.

blocks.question: Two assessors judge the same pool and agree only moderately (kappa about 0.7). What does the IR literature report happens when you swap whose judgments you use?
options: Both absolute scores and the ranking of systems change drastically
Nothing changes, because kappa above 0.67 guarantees identical scores
Absolute scores can shift considerably, but the relative order of systems mostly stays the same
Only precision changes; recall is unaffected
blocks.explain: Manning, Raghavan and Schutze summarize these experiments: the choice of judge makes a considerable absolute difference but has little impact on the relative ranking of systems. That is why test collections are used to compare systems rather than to quote absolute quality.

lessons.title: Precision, recall, and why accuracy is useless for search

blocks.md: Take one query from the collection, q1. The qrels say **5 documents are relevant** to it. Our system returns this ranked top 10: d14, d3, d27, d8, d41, d19, d5, d33, d12, d50. Of these, d14, d27, d19 and d50 are relevant. The fifth relevant document, d9, is not in the top 10 at all. This one ranking is the running example for the whole course.
Treat the first $k$ results as a set of **retrieved** documents. Two questions matter: of what I returned, how much is relevant? And of what is relevant, how much did I return?

blocks.caption: Precision is about the quality of what you showed; recall is about coverage of what exists. The recall denominator comes from the qrels, not from the run.

blocks.prompt: Suppose the collection has 10,000 documents. Compare two systems by **accuracy** (fraction of all 10,000 relevant or nonrelevant decisions that are correct): one returns our top 6, the other returns nothing at all. Which has higher accuracy?
blocks.reveal: **They tie at 0.9995.** Returning the top 6 gives 3 true positives, 3 false positives, 2 misses and 9992 true negatives: 9995 correct. Returning nothing gives 9995 true negatives and 5 misses: also 9995 correct. Because almost every document is nonrelevant, accuracy is dominated by true negatives and cannot tell a useful system from an empty one. Precision and recall ignore true negatives on purpose.

blocks.md: For a ranked list, compute both at every cutoff: **P@k** (precision at k) and **R@k** (recall at k). Walk down the ranking and watch how each changes.

blocks.title: Precision and recall at each cutoff for query q1

scenes.caption: Rank 1 is relevant: P@1 = 1/1 = 1.0, and R@1 = 1/5 = 0.2 because 5 documents are relevant in total.
Rank 2 is nonrelevant: precision drops to 0.5 but recall stays at 0.2. A miss can only lower precision; recall never decreases as k grows.
Rank 3 is relevant: both go up together, P@3 = 2/3 and R@3 = 0.4. Precision zig-zags while recall climbs in steps.
At k = 6 the third relevant document arrives: P@6 = 3/6 = 0.5, R@6 = 3/5 = 0.6.
At k = 10: P@10 = 0.4 and R@10 = 0.8. Recall cannot reach 1.0 here because d9 was never retrieved.

blocks.md: The two trade off. You can always reach recall 1.0 by returning every document, at terrible precision. A web searcher wants the first page to be precise and does not care about finding every relevant page; a paralegal doing discovery wants high recall and tolerates scrolling through junk. **R-precision** is precision at $k = R$, the number of relevant documents; here P@5 = 2/5 = 0.4.
To combine both into one number, use the **F measure**, a harmonic mean. The balanced version is $F_1$:

blocks.title: Why F1 uses a harmonic mean

scenes.caption: Returning our top 6: precision 0.5, recall 0.6. Arithmetic mean 0.55 and F1 0.545 are close when P and R are similar.
Returning all 10,000 documents: recall 1.0, precision 0.0005. The arithmetic mean still says 0.50; F1 says 0.001, correctly calling this useless. The harmonic mean stays near the smaller value.

blocks.md: P@k does not average well across queries. If a query has only 3 relevant documents, even a perfect system gets P@10 = 0.3. Also note that trec_eval's P@k pads short result lists with nonrelevant documents: retrieving 15 documents with 4 relevant gives P@20 = 4/20 = 0.2.

blocks.question: A legal team must find every contract mentioning a clause before a court deadline, and a junior reviewer will read whatever is returned. Which metric should you optimize first?
options: Precision at 1
Recall (at a generous cutoff)
Accuracy over the whole collection
Precision at 10
blocks.explain: Missing a relevant contract is the costly error, and the team will read through extra results, so recall matters most. P@1 and P@10 measure only the top of the list, and accuracy is dominated by the huge number of true negatives.

blocks.question: A query has exactly 3 relevant documents in the qrels. A perfect system ranks all 3 first. What are its P@10 and R@10?
blocks.explain: Recall is 3/3 = 1.0 because every relevant document is retrieved. Precision at 10 counts all 10 slots, and only 3 can ever be relevant, so it is 0.3 even for a perfect ranking. This is why P@k is hard to average across queries with different numbers of relevant documents.

lessons.title: Average precision, MAP and MRR: one number for a whole ranking

blocks.md: P@k forces you to pick a $k$ and ignores order inside the top $k$: a list with its relevant documents at ranks 1 and 2 gets the same P@10 as one with them at ranks 9 and 10. We want one number per query that rewards putting relevant documents early **and** finding all of them.

**Average precision (AP)** does this: every time you hit a relevant document, record the precision at that rank. Then average those precisions over **all** relevant documents in the qrels. A relevant document never retrieved contributes a precision of 0.

blocks.tex: \text{AP} = \frac{1}{R} \sum_{k \,:\, \text{doc}_k \text{ relevant}} P@k \qquad R = \text{number of relevant docs in the qrels}

blocks.title: Computing AP for query q1 step by step

scenes.caption: Start with no hits. The relevant set comes from the qrels and includes d9, which the run never retrieved.
k = 1, d14 is relevant: precision here is 1/1, so total becomes 1.0.
k = 2 is nonrelevant and adds nothing. k = 3, d27 is relevant: precision is 2/3 = 0.667, total 1.667.
k = 6, d19 is relevant: precision 3/6 = 0.5, total 2.167. The two misses at ranks 4 and 5 cost this hit some credit.
k = 10, d50 is relevant: precision 4/10 = 0.4, total 2.567.
Divide by all 5 relevant documents, not the 4 that were found. The missing d9 effectively contributes 0.

blocks.md: A common bug: dividing by the number of relevant documents *retrieved* (4) instead of all relevant documents (5). That gives 0.642 instead of 0.513 and silently rewards systems that retrieve fewer relevant documents.

Plot precision against recall after every rank and you get a saw-tooth **precision-recall curve**. TREC smooths it with **interpolated precision**: at recall level $r$, take the highest precision at any recall $\ge r$. The classic summary averages interpolated precision at 11 recall levels 0.0, 0.1, ..., 1.0.

scenes.caption: Actual (recall, precision) points at each hit: (0.2, 1.0), (0.4, 0.667), (0.6, 0.5), (0.8, 0.4). Recall levels in between have no measured precision yet.
Interpolate: each level takes the best precision at that recall or higher. Levels 0.0 to 0.2 get 1.0, 0.3 and 0.4 get 0.667, and so on.
Recall never reaches 0.9 because d9 was not retrieved, so levels 0.9 and 1.0 get 0. The 11-point average is 6.133 / 11 = 0.558.

blocks.md: **MAP** (mean average precision) is the arithmetic mean of AP over all queries, so every query counts equally no matter how many relevant documents it has. MAP became the main single number at TREC; trec_eval's documentation credits Chris Buckley with developing it after TREC 1, and notes that the name is a bit redundant since AP is already per topic.

Sometimes the user needs only **one** good answer: a question-answering box, a navigational query, a known item. Then use the **reciprocal rank** (RR): $1/\text{rank}$ of the first relevant result, and 0 if none appears. Averaged over queries it is **MRR**. For four queries whose first relevant results sit at ranks 1, 3, 2 and nowhere, MRR = (1 + 0.333 + 0.5 + 0) / 4 = 0.458. The MS MARCO passage ranking task reports MRR@10: anything below rank 10 scores 0.

blocks.question: In q1, the relevant document d50 moves from rank 10 up to rank 7, and nothing else changes. Which metrics change?
options: P@10 and AP both increase
Only RR changes
AP increases (0.513 to 0.548); P@10 and RR stay the same
Nothing changes, because the same documents are in the top 10
blocks.explain: P@10 still counts 4 relevant in 10 slots, and RR depends only on the first relevant document, which is still d14 at rank 1. AP rewards the earlier hit: precision at that hit goes from 4/10 to 4/7, so AP becomes (1 + 0.667 + 0.5 + 0.571) / 5 = 0.548.

blocks.question: You evaluate a search box that jumps the user straight to a product page (each query has exactly one correct product). Which metric best matches the user's experience?
options: MRR
Recall@1000
MAP over all relevant products
11-point interpolated precision
blocks.explain: With exactly one right answer, what matters is how high it appears, which is what reciprocal rank measures. Recall@1000 ignores position. With a single relevant document AP equals RR anyway, and the recall-level machinery of 11-point precision adds nothing.

lessons.title: Graded relevance and nDCG: rewarding the best result first

blocks.md: Binary labels throw information away. In q1, d27 is the perfect answer, d19 and d9 are good, and d14 and d50 are only marginally useful. Give them **graded** labels: 3 (highly relevant), 2, 1, and 0 (nonrelevant). AP cannot see these grades: it would score our ranking 0.513 whether the perfect answer sits at rank 1 or at rank 3.

**Discounted cumulative gain** (DCG), introduced by Jarvelin and Kekalainen (SIGIR 2000, extended with the normalized nDCG in ACM TOIS 2002), adds up a **gain** for each result, reduced by a **discount** that grows with rank, because users are less likely to look further down. trec_eval's default uses the grade itself as the gain:

blocks.caption: g_i is the grade of the document at rank i. IDCG is the DCG of the ideal ranking: all judged documents sorted by grade, best first.

blocks.title: DCG@10 for q1, then the ideal ranking

scenes.caption: Our ranking's grades at ranks 1 to 10, with the discount for each rank. Rank 1 is undiscounted; rank 10 keeps only 0.289 of its gain.
Multiply grade by discount. The grade-3 document at rank 3 is worth 3 x 0.5 = 1.5; at rank 1 it would have been worth 3.0.
Running sum: DCG@5 = 2.500 and DCG@10 = 3.501. On its own this number has no fixed scale, so it cannot be compared across queries.
The ideal ranking sorts every judged document by grade, including d9 (grade 2) that our run missed: 3, 2, 2, 1, 1. Its DCG@10 is 6.079.
Normalize: nDCG@10 = 3.501 / 6.079 = 0.576, and nDCG@5 = 2.500 / 6.079 = 0.411. A perfect ranking always scores 1.

blocks.title: How much one result is worth at each rank

scenes.caption: Grade 1: both gain forms coincide, since 2^1 - 1 = 1. The log discount falls much more gently than reciprocal rank, so rank 10 still counts for 0.29.
Grade 3: the exponential form gives 7 instead of 3, so one highly relevant document outweighs several marginal ones. Which form you use changes the score.

blocks.prompt: Swap d14 (grade 1) and d27 (grade 3), so the perfect answer is at rank 1. What happens to AP and to nDCG@10?
blocks.reveal: **AP is unchanged at 0.513**: both documents count as relevant, and relevant documents still sit at ranks 1, 3, 6 and 10. **nDCG@10 rises from 0.576 to 0.740** (linear gain), or from 0.523 to 0.790 with exponential gain. Only a graded metric can tell that the best answer moved to the top.

blocks.md: IDCG must come from **all** judged documents in the qrels, not from re-sorting the documents your run retrieved. Re-sorting only the retrieved ones gives IDCG 5.193 and nDCG@10 = 0.674 instead of 0.576, and hides the fact that the run missed d9 entirely. trec_eval builds the ideal from the qrels.

Two gain conventions are in common use: trec_eval uses the grade itself ($g_i$), while the Manning, Raghavan and Schutze textbook writes the gain as $2^{g_i} - 1$. For q1 they give nDCG@10 of 0.576 and 0.523. Always state the gain and the cutoff when you report nDCG. BEIR, a widely used zero-shot retrieval benchmark, reports nDCG@10 on every dataset because it works with both binary and graded judgments.
nDCG@k answers: what fraction of the best achievable discounted gain did the top k results capture? It is the default when labels are graded and users look mostly at the first page.

blocks.question: Two teams score the same run on the same qrels and report nDCG@10 of 0.576 and 0.523. Neither has a bug. What is the most likely explanation?
options: One used a natural log instead of log base 2 in the discount
One used linear gain g and the other exponential gain 2^g - 1
One computed nDCG@5 by mistake
nDCG is randomized, so small differences are expected
blocks.explain: These are exactly q1's values under the two gain conventions. Changing the log base alone would not change nDCG at all, since the same constant factor appears in DCG and IDCG and cancels. nDCG@5 is 0.411 here, and nDCG is deterministic.

blocks.question: A reranker reorders a run's top 10 so the grades go from 1,0,3,0,0,2,0,0,0,1 to 3,2,1,1,0,0,0,0,0,0. What nDCG@10 does it reach, and why not 1.0?
options: 1.0, because the top 10 is now in perfect order
Below 1.0, because d9 (grade 2) is still missing and IDCG includes it
Below 1.0, because nDCG penalizes reordering
Exactly 0.576, because the same documents are retrieved
blocks.explain: Reordering cannot add documents. The ideal ranking from the qrels is 3,2,2,1,1, so this list (3,2,1,1) still loses gain for the missing grade-2 document. Only a better first-stage retriever that finds d9 could reach 1.0.

lessons.title: Comparing systems honestly: judgment holes, variance, online tests

blocks.md: You now have metrics. The hard part is using them to decide whether system B really beats system A. Three things routinely mislead people: **unjudged documents**, **per-query variance**, and **tool defaults**.

**Holes in the judgments.** Pools come from the systems that existed when the collection was built. A new kind of system can retrieve relevant documents that nobody judged, and they count as nonrelevant. The BEIR authors measured this on TREC-COVID: they judged 980 extra query-document pairs that various systems put in their top 10 but annotators had never seen, then rescored everything.

blocks.title: TREC-COVID nDCG@10 before and after filling judgment holes

scenes.caption: With the original judgments, the dense retriever ANCE (0.654) looks slightly worse than BM25 (0.656). Lexical systems had 6.4% and 2.8% unjudged top-10 hits; TAS-B had 31.8%.
After judging the holes, lexical systems barely move (BM25 +0.012, docT5query +0.001) but ANCE jumps +0.081 to 0.735 and beats BM25. The pool was biased toward lexical matching.

blocks.md: **Per-query variance.** One system's AP typically ranges widely across queries (Manning et al. cite 0.1 to 0.7), and scores for one query usually agree more across systems than scores for different queries within one system. A mean over a few queries is therefore noisy; about 50 information needs is the usual rule-of-thumb minimum. Look at the per-query differences, not just the means.

blocks.title: Per-query AP for systems A and B (illustrative)

scenes.caption: Illustrative numbers. MAP for A is 0.368 and for B is 0.430, so B looks 17% better on average.
But B is worse on 6 of the 8 queries. Its whole advantage comes from q4, where A scored 0.10 and B scored 0.70.
Drop q4 and A wins, 0.406 to 0.391. A paired t-test over the 8 differences gives p = 0.44 and a sign test p = 0.29: no evidence that B is better in general.

blocks.md: Compare systems with a **paired** test over queries (each query is scored by both systems, so test the per-query differences): the paired t-test, the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, or the sign test. Each returns a **p-value**: the probability of seeing a difference at least this large if the two systems were really equally good. A small p-value (conventionally below 0.05) is evidence of a real difference; p = 0.44 is not. Then read the failing queries; a single outlier like q4 often reveals a bug or a judgment hole rather than a better model.

blocks.code:
# per-query scores (-q), and count queries with no results as 0 (-c)
trec_eval -q -c -m map -m ndcg_cut.10 -m recip_rank qrels.txt run.txt

# graded qrels: treat only grade >= 2 as relevant for binary metrics
trec_eval -l 2 -m map qrels.txt run.txt
blocks.caption: trec_eval flags from its own help text. -l sets the minimum grade counted as relevant (default 1).

blocks.md: By default trec_eval silently ignores queries for which a run retrieved nothing, so a system that crashes on hard queries can score higher. Pass -c to average over every query in the qrels, with missing queries scored 0.

**Offline is not the whole story.** Judges cannot always guess real users' intents, and judging is slow and costly. Production search teams therefore also run **online** tests on live traffic. Besides A/B tests, a common method is **interleaving**: merge the rankings of A and B into one list shown to a user, and credit each system with the clicks on its documents. Chapelle, Joachims, Radlinski and Yue validated interleaving at scale on two commercial search engines and a scientific literature search system, comparing it with judgment-based metrics.

A test collection is a measuring instrument with known biases. Report the metric, cutoff and gain you used, look at per-query results, test significance with paired tests, and be suspicious when a genuinely new kind of system loses on an old pool.

blocks.question: Your new dense retriever scores 0.05 nDCG@10 below BM25 on a collection whose pool was built mostly from lexical systems a decade ago. What should you do before concluding it is worse?
options: Nothing; nDCG@10 already accounts for unjudged documents
Switch to P@10, which is not affected by unjudged documents
Measure how many of its top-10 documents are unjudged, and judge a sample of them
Re-run with trec_eval -J and report that number as the true score
blocks.explain: Unjudged documents count as nonrelevant in nDCG and in P@10 alike. Measuring the hole rate and judging a sample, as BEIR did on TREC-COVID, tells you whether the gap is real. The -J flag drops unjudged documents, which inflates scores in a different way and is not comparable.

blocks.question: B beats A on MAP, 0.43 versus 0.37, over 8 queries. B wins on 2 queries and loses on 6. Which conclusion is justified?
options: B is better: MAP is the standard measure
Not established yet: check per-query differences with a paired test and add queries
A is better because it wins more queries
They are identical because 8 queries is too few to compute MAP
blocks.explain: A mean driven by one or two queries is fragile, and with 8 queries neither a t-test (p = 0.44) nor a sign test (p = 0.29) supports a general claim. Counting wins alone is also not a valid conclusion. Use more queries (about 50 is a common minimum) and a paired test.
